heuristics.rule: Evaluate total compensation as Base + Bonus + Equity + Benefits + Growth, not just base salary
heuristics.condition: When comparing offers from different companies or negotiating a new offer
heuristics.action: Calculate the annualized value of each component separately, including RSU vesting schedule, bonus percentage of base, and 401K match, before comparing
heuristics.because: The author explicitly states that focusing only on salary causes Chinese international students to leave value on the table during offer negotiation

heuristics.rule: Account for equity refresh when calculating long-term compensation at a company
heuristics.condition: When evaluating whether to stay at a company or accept a competing offer after 2+ years
heuristics.action: Ask the recruiter or hiring manager explicitly about the equity refresh policy and timeline before deciding
heuristics.because: Without equity refresh, a 4-year RSU grant creates a cliff where compensation drops sharply in years 3-4, making the employee an easy target for competing offers — the author calls this a structural retention problem

heuristics.rule: When leaving a company with unvested options, ask the next employer to cover exercise costs in the sign-on bonus
heuristics.condition: When you have vested ISO/NQSO options that must be exercised within 90 days of leaving
heuristics.action: Quantify the total exercise cost and request that amount (or partial coverage) as a sign-on bonus from the new employer
heuristics.because: The author states this is an established negotiation tactic in Silicon Valley, and some employers fully cover the cost to secure the candidate

heuristics.rule: If leaving a company before year-end bonus is paid, adjust 401K contribution to maximize employer match on the bonus payout
heuristics.condition: When you plan to leave a job and your current employer's 401K match rate significantly exceeds the new employer's
heuristics.action: One month before the bonus payout, increase your 401K personal contribution percentage to capture as much of the bonus as possible under the higher match rate
heuristics.because: The author explicitly describes this tactic as capable of generating several thousand dollars of additional personal asset growth due to pre-tax compounding

heuristics.rule: For back-weighted vesting schedules (e.g., Amazon 5/15/20/20 or Snapchat 10/20/30/40), calculate expected tenure-weighted value before accepting
heuristics.condition: When an offer contains a vesting schedule where later years have disproportionately larger grants
heuristics.action: Model out your expected tenure (e.g., 2 years vs. 4 years) and calculate what percentage of total equity you would actually realize, then negotiate accordingly
heuristics.because: The author explicitly labels these structures as 'golden handcuffs' and says they are unfair to employees who leave before full vesting

decision_factors.why_it_matters: A back-weighted schedule (e.g., Snapchat 10/20/30/40) means an employee who leaves at year 2 captures only 30% of total grant value, while a uniform schedule (25% per year) would yield 50% — a massive difference in realized compensation
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Read the offer letter carefully for the vest percentage per year; if not specified, ask HR directly. Compare to standard 4-year/1-year-cliff model

decision_factors.factor: Geographic location and state tax rate
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Companies adjust compensation based on local labor market demand and state tax burden. A Seattle or Austin offer may have lower nominal comp than a San Francisco equivalent, but higher take-home due to absence of state income tax
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Compare after-tax income using state tax rates; California has 13%+ marginal state income tax vs. 0% in Washington and Texas

decision_factors.factor: Company stage (public vs. pre-IPO vs. early startup) for equity valuation
decision_factors.why_it_matters: RSUs at a public company have immediate liquid value; options at an early startup may take 9+ years to become liquid and carry risk of total loss
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Determine if the company is public, pre-IPO, or early-stage; ask about liquidity timeline and exercise window if leaving

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Without equity refresh, total comp declines significantly in years 3-4 of employment, making the employee vulnerable to being poached by any company offering above base salary
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask HR: 'Does the company have an equity refresh program? When does it kick in — at 1 year, 2 years? How is the refresh amount determined?'

decision_factors.why_it_matters: A 50% match vs. a 10% match on the same base salary represents thousands of dollars annually in pre-tax wealth accumulation with compounding advantages
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask the exact match percentage, the cap (e.g., match up to 6% of salary), and whether it's based on base salary only or total compensation

decision_factors.factor: Option exercise window after leaving (90 days vs. extended)
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Standard 90-day exercise window forces employees to come up with potentially tens of thousands of dollars cash within 3 months or forfeit vested options; extended windows (3-7 years) at some companies eliminate this pressure
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check offer letter or equity plan documents for post-termination exercise period; ask HR if not specified

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting RSUs at a startup that then goes bankrupt
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Because RSU income is taxed as ordinary income at vest time, employees who vest RSUs at a company that subsequently fails have already paid income tax on shares that are now worthless — a permanent loss with no tax recovery equivalent to the option holder's ability to simply not exercise
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Employees at pre-IPO companies that grant RSUs rather than options, particularly those who vest shortly before a company downturn

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Staying at a company until the full 4-year RSU cliff without negotiating equity refresh
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: At the 2-year mark, the employee's forward-looking compensation drops sharply (from e.g., 125K/year to 100K/year projected), making them financially vulnerable to being poached — but many employees don't realize this until they do the math themselves
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Mid-level employees who accepted strong initial RSU packages but never asked about or received equity refresh grants

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Leaving a company with vested ISO options without planning the exercise
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The 90-day post-termination exercise window requires immediate cash outlay of potentially $10K–$100K+ to exercise vested options, with AMT tax exposure on top. Many employees forfeit valuable vested options simply because they lack the liquidity
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Early employees at fast-growing private companies who have accumulated significant vested options but limited liquid savings

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Exercising ISOs and holding shares to qualify for long-term capital gains treatment
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Holding exercised ISO shares triggers AMT (Alternative Minimum Tax) liability in the exercise year, even though no cash has been received — creating a tax bill without liquidity to pay it
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: High-earning employees at well-valued private companies who exercise large ISO blocks hoping to convert to long-term capital gains

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Choosing a role based on nominal RSU grant value stated in the offer letter
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The number of shares is not fixed at offer time — it is determined on the first day of employment based on the stock price that day. If the stock price rises between offer acceptance and start date, the employee receives fewer shares than mentally modeled
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: First-time offer recipients at public tech companies who do not understand that dollar value is fixed but share count floats

failure_patterns.pattern: Evaluating an offer based only on base salary without modeling annualized equity value
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Base salary is the most salient, immediately legible number; equity vesting schedules require multi-step calculation that most first-time job seekers haven't been taught
failure_patterns.consequence: Candidates accept lower total compensation packages or negotiate the wrong component, leaving significant money on the table
warning_signs: Candidate asks only 'what is the base salary?' and stops there
Candidate compares offers by base salary alone without building a year-by-year compensation model

failure_patterns.pattern: Forfeiting vested options at departure because the 90-day exercise window is not planned for
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Employees focus on the new job excitement and don't calculate the cash needed to exercise options until it's too late; the 90-day clock starts immediately at termination
failure_patterns.consequence: Potentially tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars in vested compensation permanently forfeited
warning_signs: Employee is leaving a company without having checked the post-termination exercise period
Employee has not calculated the cash required to exercise all vested options

failure_patterns.pattern: Not asking new employer to cover option exercise costs as part of sign-on negotiation
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates don't know this is a negotiable item; they assume sign-on bonus is a fixed goodwill gesture, not a tool to compensate for leaving money behind
failure_patterns.consequence: Employee either forfeits vested options (loss of asset) or funds the exercise personally (cash strain) when the new employer could have covered it
warning_signs: Candidate mentions they have unvested equity or options costs but doesn't raise it with new employer
Candidate accepts sign-on bonus without disclosing what they are leaving behind at current company

failure_patterns.pattern: Ignoring equity refresh when evaluating long-term compensation trajectory at a company
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Equity refresh is almost never mentioned in the offer letter; candidates assume the original grant represents the steady-state compensation indefinitely
failure_patterns.consequence: Employee reaches year 3-4 with declining forward compensation and no leverage to negotiate internally, or is blindsided when their total comp drops
warning_signs: Candidate can state their initial RSU grant but cannot describe the refresh policy
Candidate has been at a company 2+ years and has never received an equity refresh discussion in performance review

diagnostic_questions.question: What is the vesting schedule structure — is it uniform (25% per year) or back-weighted?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Back-weighted schedules disproportionately reward long tenure and punish early departure; they change the break-even tenure calculation significantly
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If back-weighted, model the equity captured at your expected tenure (e.g., 2 years) and compare to what a uniform schedule would yield — then negotiate for a more favorable structure or higher total grant
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If uniform, standard 4-year/1-year-cliff model applies; focus negotiation on total grant size and refresh policy

diagnostic_questions.question: Does the company have an equity refresh program, and when does it start?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the company is committed to retaining employees past the initial grant period; absence of refresh means compensation cliff risk at year 3-4
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Ask: how is the refresh amount determined? Is it tied to performance review, market benchmarking, or discretionary? How frequently is it granted?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Factor in the compensation cliff when evaluating the offer; the effective annual compensation drops significantly in years 3-4 without refresh

diagnostic_questions.question: If this is an option grant at a private company, what is the post-termination exercise window?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the employee will face a cash-and-AMT trap if they leave before liquidity; standard 90 days is highly restrictive, extended windows (3-7 years) are employee-friendly
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If extended window (3+ years), the options have more option value — you can wait for a favorable liquidity event without being forced to exercise immediately
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If standard 90 days, build an exercise cost estimate (shares × strike price) and plan for this as a potential liability when leaving

diagnostic_questions.question: Is the equity grant in the form of RSUs, ISO options, or NQSO options?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: The tax treatment differs materially: RSUs are taxed as ordinary income at vest; ISOs have AMT exposure but potential capital gains treatment; NQSOs are taxed as ordinary income at exercise on the spread
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If RSUs at a public company: model the withholding mechanism and plan for share-based tax withholding reducing the number of shares received
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If options at a private company: evaluate liquidity timeline, strike price relative to current 409A valuation, and exercise cost before accepting

industry_realities.common_belief: The RSU grant amount in your offer letter is the number of shares you'll receive
industry_realities.actual_reality: The offer letter states a dollar value; the actual share count is calculated on your first day of employment based on the stock's closing price that day (or a recent average, per company policy). The share count is not known at offer acceptance
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should model scenarios where the stock price moves between signing and start date, and should not fixate on a specific share count until Day 1

industry_realities.common_belief: When RSUs vest, you receive the full value of the shares in cash or stock
industry_realities.actual_reality: RSU vesting is a taxable event treated as ordinary W-2 income. The company withholds shares to cover estimated tax (often 35-40%+ of vest value), so the employee receives significantly fewer shares than vested. Some of the withheld amount may be refunded in cash if the withheld shares slightly over-cover the tax
industry_realities.implication: Employees should calculate after-tax RSU value using their marginal income tax rate, not the face value of the vest — the actual cash/stock received is 55-65% of the gross vest value

industry_realities.common_belief: RSUs are always better than options because options require you to spend money
industry_realities.actual_reality: At an early-stage startup that fails, RSU holders lose more: they already paid ordinary income tax on vested RSUs, while option holders can simply decline to exercise and lose nothing beyond foregone opportunity cost
industry_realities.implication: For early-stage startup compensation, options (especially ISOs) offer asymmetric downside protection that RSUs do not — the choice between them depends on company stage and failure probability

industry_realities.common_belief: Equity refresh is part of the offer and will be clearly explained
industry_realities.actual_reality: Equity refresh is almost never mentioned in the offer letter. It is an ongoing employment benefit governed by internal policies that can change, and its terms are determined by performance reviews and management discretion, not contract
industry_realities.implication: Candidates must proactively ask about refresh policies before accepting; they cannot rely on the offer letter to represent steady-state long-term compensation

industry_realities.common_belief: ESPP is a major wealth-building vehicle like RSUs
industry_realities.actual_reality: ESPP is closer to a company benefit (like 401K match) than a primary wealth-building tool. The author explicitly states it rarely generates significant wealth growth; if you believe in the company's stock, you can buy it on the open market without being employed there
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should not over-weight ESPP in compensation comparisons; focus negotiation energy on base, RSU grant, and refresh policy instead

industry_realities.common_belief: A candidate leveled as Senior must earn more than a Junior at the same company
industry_realities.actual_reality: Due to offer negotiation dynamics and external market benchmarking, a strong Junior candidate can receive a higher base salary than a newly-leveled Senior if the Junior's external offers or skills justify it. Level and salary are set through partially independent processes
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should negotiate both level and base independently; accepting a level bump without negotiating base can leave money on the table

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How they read an offer letter
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Looks at base salary and maybe the total RSU dollar value; accepts these numbers at face value as representing annual income
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Builds a year-by-year compensation model including vesting schedule, bonus percentage, 401K match, and equity refresh; computes after-tax take-home for each component
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Two offers with identical base salaries can differ by $20K–$50K annually in realized total compensation due to equity structure and benefit differences

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Asks if the base salary can be increased; treats the equity grant as fixed
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Negotiates across all levers: base, sign-on, RSU grant size, vesting schedule, equity refresh timing, and relocation/exercise cost coverage
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Experienced negotiators extract value from components that naive candidates don't know are negotiable, often achieving equivalent outcomes through non-base channels that are easier for companies to approve

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How they think about equity at private companies
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Calculates paper value of options as (current valuation × share count) and treats it as real income
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Discounts private company equity heavily for illiquidity, failure probability, and dilution; models realistic exit scenarios and timeline; evaluates exercise cost and AMT risk before accepting
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Overvaluing illiquid private equity leads to accepting below-market cash compensation; undervaluing it leads to missing legitimate upside at high-quality pre-IPO companies

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Views the 4-year RSU grant as a static feature of employment; doesn't think about what happens when it fully vests
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Proactively asks about equity refresh before joining; monitors their forward-looking compensation trajectory annually; uses upcoming equity cliff as negotiation leverage for refresh grants or competing offers
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Employees who don't manage their equity cliff become easy poaching targets and may leave significant money on the table by not negotiating refresh grants

community_misconceptions.misconception: RSU share count is locked in at the time you receive your offer
community_misconceptions.why_believed: The offer letter specifies a dollar value which feels like a contract; candidates naturally assume the share count is also determined at that point
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: Share count is calculated on the employee's first day of employment based on the stock price that day (or a recent rolling average per company policy); only the dollar value commitment is made at offer time
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Candidates who model compensation based on an assumed share count may be surprised — positively or negatively — when the actual share count is set at a different stock price

community_misconceptions.misconception: When RSUs vest, you get to keep all the shares
community_misconceptions.why_believed: The vesting event feels like receiving a paycheck; the concept of shares being withheld for taxes is non-intuitive for people unfamiliar with equity compensation
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: RSU vesting triggers ordinary income tax; the company withholds a portion of the vested shares (typically 30-40%) and sells them to cover the estimated tax liability. The employee receives the remainder
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Employees who expect to receive 2,500 shares at vesting may actually receive ~1,500 shares; planning for large share accumulations or stock concentration management will be off if this is not understood

community_misconceptions.misconception: Options are worse than RSUs because you have to pay to exercise them
community_misconceptions.why_believed: The requirement to spend money to exercise options feels like a disadvantage versus RSUs which are 'free'; the downside protection of options is non-intuitive
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: At failing companies, RSU holders have already paid ordinary income tax on vested shares that are now worthless — a real economic loss. Option holders can simply not exercise, losing only the opportunity cost. Options provide asymmetric downside protection that RSUs lack
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Candidates at risky early-stage startups who discount option grants in favor of RSU grants may actually be accepting worse risk-adjusted compensation

community_misconceptions.misconception: Bonus is paid in December at year end
community_misconceptions.why_believed: The term 'annual bonus' and 'year-end bonus' implies payment coincides with the calendar year end
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: Annual bonuses in US tech companies are typically paid in January through March of the following year, so they are taxed as income in the year they are received (the new year), not the performance year
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Employees who plan to leave in December may miss their bonus entirely if they don't understand the actual payout timing; those who leave in January after receiving the bonus correctly capture it

real_case_outcomes.situation: Employee A joins Company X with 100K base + 100K RSU over 4 years (25K/year); two years later approaches the compensation review with no equity refresh granted
real_case_outcomes.decision: Employee did not ask about equity refresh at offer time and did not proactively negotiate for a refresh grant in performance reviews
real_case_outcomes.outcome: At the 2-year mark, the employee's forward-looking annual compensation drops from 125K to 100K for years 3-4, making any competing offer above 100K base financially attractive and giving the employer minimal retention leverage
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Equity refresh is a critical retention and compensation tool that must be proactively negotiated — both at offer time (ask about the policy) and at performance reviews (ask for a refresh grant). Ignoring it creates a self-inflicted compensation cliff

real_case_outcomes.situation: Silicon Valley employee leaves a company with significant vested ISO options; strike price is $1, current 409A valuation is $11, with 10,000 vested shares
real_case_outcomes.decision: Must decide whether to exercise 10,000 ISOs within 90 days of departure, requiring $10,000 cash outlay plus potential AMT exposure on $100,000 paper gain
real_case_outcomes.outcome: The author frames this as a genuine financial trap; employees who lack liquidity either forfeit the vested options or are forced to exercise under pressure without optimal tax planning
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Before leaving a company with vested options, calculate the full exercise cost (shares × strike price) plus potential AMT liability, and negotiate with the new employer to cover this cost via a sign-on bonus if possible — some Silicon Valley companies will fully cover this amount to secure the candidate

psychological_barriers.trigger: First-time offer recipients asking 'is this offer good?' without specifying any components other than base salary
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Anchoring bias combined with information overload; the base salary is the most legible number so it becomes the proxy for total offer quality
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Candidate evaluates and negotiates only the base salary, treating equity, bonus structure, and refresh policy as fixed background noise
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Force a full compensation breakdown exercise: 'Write out base + expected bonus + year 1 RSU vest + 401K match. Now do the same for year 3 and year 4. Does your total comp hold up, or does it cliff?' This makes the multi-component structure visceral

psychological_barriers.trigger: International students (F-1/OPT) asking whether they can negotiate at all given visa dependency on the employer
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Catastrophizing: the student perceives any negotiation as risking offer rescission, which conflates with visa status loss — a disproportionate fear response
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Student accepts first offer without negotiating any component; may not even ask clarifying questions about equity structure for fear of appearing difficult
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Reframe the risk: 'Companies spend $20K–$30K recruiting you. Rescinding an offer for asking a reasonable compensation question has almost never been documented. The risk of not negotiating is guaranteed undercompensation; the risk of negotiating is near-zero.' This recalibrates the probability assessment

psychological_barriers.trigger: Candidates who feel overwhelmed by equity complexity and say 'I'll just focus on the base salary since I understand that'
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Complexity aversion leading to motivated reasoning — the candidate avoids the equity analysis because it's cognitively demanding, not because it's unimportant
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Candidate systematically underweights or ignores equity in compensation comparisons, leading to choices that favor simpler (often lower total comp) offers
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Reduce the equity calculation to a single number: 'Annual equity value = total grant ÷ 4 (for standard vesting). Add that to your base. Now compare.' Make the calculation trivially simple to overcome the avoidance

reframing_moves.original_framing: How much is my RSU worth?
reframing_moves.reframe: Your RSU grant is a dollar commitment, not a share commitment — and the after-tax value is what you actually receive. Model it as: (vest value at that day's price) × (1 - your marginal tax rate) = actual shares/cash received
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Shifts the candidate from treating equity as a fixed asset to treating it as a variable cash flow with tax drag — a more accurate mental model that prevents both over- and under-valuation
reframing_moves.example_language: 当你vest RSU时，那笔收入是算作个人基本工资收入类别上税的，假设你个人税率是40%, 你实际收到的是60%的价值

reframing_moves.original_framing: My offer says 100K base + 100K RSU over 4 years, so I'll make 125K per year
reframing_moves.reframe: That's only true for the first two years. What does your compensation look like in year 3 and year 4 — and is there an equity refresh? Without it, you're projecting a future pay cut
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Forces the candidate to think in a forward trajectory rather than a static annual snapshot, revealing the compensation cliff that is invisible in naive year-1 analysis
reframing_moves.example_language: 假设A接了Offer并在X公司开开心心地奋斗了两年，有一天突然意识到那时自己未来四年每年的收益为 (125k, 125k, 100k, 100k)

reframing_moves.original_framing: Options are risky because I have to pay for them, while RSUs are free
reframing_moves.reframe: RSUs are not free — you pay income tax on them at vest. If the company fails after you vest RSUs, you've permanently overpaid taxes on worthless shares. Options let you choose not to exercise, so your downside is zero. The question isn't 'which one costs money' but 'which one has better risk-adjusted value at this company's stage'
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Corrects the framing error by making the tax cost of RSUs visible and introducing the concept of optionality value — changing the decision axis from 'which requires cash' to 'which has better expected value given company risk'
reframing_moves.example_language: 如果是持有RSU的员工，因为RSU grant时已经交了一波个人所得税，公司倒闭时这些RSU就一文不值了，意味着她凭空多交了那么多个人所得税
